questions.stem: A node of a singly linked list holds:
options: a value and a reference to the next node
a value and its index in the list
a value and references to every later node
only a value; the list stores the order separately
questions.explanation: The order is in the links themselves; there are no indices (b) and no separate order (d).

questions.stem: Reading ll[i] on a linked list of n nodes costs:
questions.explanation: Follow next i times from head: O(i), O(n) in the worst case.

questions.stem: push_front costs:
questions.explanation: Two reference assignments, independent of n. "Amortised" (c) describes the dynamic array's append, not this.

questions.stem: append on a singly linked list without a tail reference costs:
questions.explanation: It must walk to the last node first. A tail reference makes it O(1).

questions.stem: Which operation is O(1) on a linked list but O(n) on a dynamic array?
questions.explanation: Front insertion: two references here; every element shifts in an array.

questions.stem: Which operation is O(1) on a dynamic array but O(n) on a linked list?
questions.explanation: Indexing: address arithmetic in an array, a walk in a list. len (d) is O(1) in both — because the list keeps _size.

questions.stem: In push_front, why must new.next = self.head come before self.head = new?
options: Python evaluates assignments right to left
Done the other way round, new.next would point to new itself and the rest of the list would be lost
It is only a style convention
questions.explanation: After self.head = new, new.next = self.head makes the node point at itself, and the old first node is no longer referenced by anything. Python evaluates each assignment's right-hand side first (a), but that is not the reason for the order of two separate statements.

questions.stem: To remove a node from a singly linked list, you need a reference to:
questions.explanation: Only the predecessor holds the reference that must be redirected around the removed node.

questions.stem: Which node is the special case in remove(value) without a sentinel?
options: none — there is no special case
questions.explanation: The head has no predecessor, so it is removed by moving head instead.

questions.stem:
What is the running time of this loop over a linked list of n nodes?

for i in range(len(ll)):
    total += ll[i]
questions.explanation: Each ll[i] walks i steps from the head: 0 + 1 + … + (n-1). Use for value in ll: for one O(n) walk.

questions.stem: Why is len(ll) O(1) in dsa/linked_list.py?
options: Python caches the length of every object
The list keeps _size up to date in every method that adds or removes
Linked lists have a fixed size
It is not — it walks the list
questions.explanation: A stored count, updated by push_front, append, insert_at, pop_front and remove. Forget one, and len lies.

questions.stem: Reversing a linked list in place needs how much extra space?
questions.explanation: Three references — prev, node and the saved next — whatever n is.

questions.stem: On 64-bit CPython, a Node with __slots__ takes about 48 bytes. One slot of an array of references takes:
options: it depends on the value stored
questions.explanation: One 8-byte reference per slot; the node is six times larger.

questions.stem: A doubly linked list can do in O(1) what a singly linked one cannot:
options: remove a node you already hold a reference to
questions.explanation: With prev in each node, the node itself gives you its predecessor. Indexing (a) and search (c) are still O(n).

questions.stem: What is a sentinel (dummy) node for?
options: to mark the end of the list instead of None
to give every real node a predecessor, removing the special case for the head
questions.explanation: With a permanent node before the first real one, removing the first real node looks exactly like removing any other.

questions.stem: A singly linked list with a tail reference. Removing the last node costs:
options: O(1) — the tail points at it
O(n) — the new last node must be found from the head
questions.explanation: After removing the last node, _tail must move to its predecessor, and only a walk from the head finds it in a singly linked list.

questions.stem: Python's collections.deque is implemented as:
options: a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks
a singly linked list of single values
questions.explanation: Blocks give array-like memory efficiency; the links give O(1) at both ends.

questions.stem: Why does the traversal loop test while node is not None: rather than while node.next is not None:?
options: The second version stops on the last node, so it never visits it — and crashes on an empty list
node.next is not allowed in a condition
questions.explanation: It is the standard off-by-one: node.next is not None is the right test only when you want to stop on the last node (to append after it).

questions.stem: After a = Node(1), b = Node(2, a), c = Node(3, b), what is c.next.next.value?
questions.explanation: c.next is b, and b.next is a, whose value is 1.

questions.stem: In Python, what happens to a node that nothing refers to any more?
options: it stays in memory until the program ends
questions.explanation: Unreachable objects are reclaimed automatically. del (b) only removes a name.

questions.stem: To insert a new node at index i ≥ 1, you walk to the node at index:
questions.explanation: The node at i − 1 is the one whose next must change. Index 0 is push_front.

questions.stem: Where in this course do short linked lists appear inside another structure?
options: as the chains of a hash table
questions.explanation: ChainingHashMap (Week 13) stores an Array of chains of Entry nodes.

questions.stem:
What is printed?

ll = LinkedList([1, 2, 3, 4])
node = ll.head.next
node.next = node.next.next
print(list(ll), len(ll))
questions.explanation: node is the second node, and node.next = node.next.next skips node 3, so the walk finds [1, 2, 4]. But the change bypassed the list's methods, so _size was never decremented and len still says 4. (a) is what remove(3) would leave. (b) skips the wrong node.

questions.stem: On a list of 6 nodes, insert_at(4, x) runs. How many times does prev = prev.next run?
questions.explanation: prev must stop on the node before the gap, at index 3. It starts at index 0, so range(index - 1) moves it 3 times. 4 (c) is one step too far: the new node would land at index 5.

questions.stem: ll = LinkedList([1, 2, 3]). Which call raises IndexError?
questions.explanation: Reading allows 0 <= index < len, so ll[3] is out of range. Inserting allows 0 <= index <= len, so (b) is a legal append at the end and (d) is push_front. ll[-1] (c) is 3: __getitem__ adds _size to a negative index.

questions.stem: In a list with a sentinel node, the list is empty when:
questions.explanation: The sentinel is permanent. It is never None (a) and never removed (d), and its value is meaningless (c). The first real node is sentinel.next, so no real node means sentinel.next is None.

questions.stem: In a doubly linked list, x is a node that is neither the first nor the last. Which two assignments remove it from the list?
questions.explanation: The node before x must point past it, and the node after x must point back past it. (a) and (b) change only x's own references, which leaves the neighbours still linked to x. (d) makes each neighbour point at itself.

questions.stem: A new node is inserted between two neighbouring nodes a and b of a doubly linked list. How many references must be set, counting the new node's own?
questions.explanation: new.prev = a, new.next = b, a.next = new and b.prev = new. A singly linked list needs only two of these, which is the "twice the bookkeeping" of the doubly linked list.

questions.stem:
A student adds _tail to the list. Their append decides "empty" by testing self._tail is None, and their pop_front updates head and _size but never _tail. What does this print?

ll = LinkedList([7])
ll.pop_front()
ll.append(5)
print(list(ll), len(ll))
questions.explanation: After pop_front, head is None but _tail still refers to the old node 7. append sees a tail that is not None, so it links 5 after that dead node and never sets head. The walk from head finds nothing, while _size went from 0 to 1. It fails silently and raises no error (d). Every method that can empty the list must clear _tail.

questions.stem: reverse() runs on 1 → 2 → 3. After the first pass of the loop body, what is the state?
questions.explanation: The body saves following = Node(2), turns Node(1).next round to prev, which is None, then steps forward: prev becomes Node(1) and current becomes Node(2). (d) forgets that the link was turned. (c) is the state after the second pass.

questions.stem: Suppose insert_at had no index == 0 case and went straight to the walk. What would insert_at(0, 9) do to [1, 2, 3]?
options: give [1, 9, 2, 3]: range(-1) is empty, so the node goes after the head
questions.explanation: range(0 - 1) is empty, so prev stays on the head, and the new node is spliced in after it, at index 1. No error is raised (b), and the list is wrong. On an empty list prev is None, and prev.next raises AttributeError. Position 0 has no node before it, so the head itself must change: that is push_front.

questions.stem: ll = LinkedList([4, 2, 4]), then ll.remove(4). Now list(ll) is:
questions.explanation: remove stops at the first node holding the value: here it is the head (the special case), so head moves on and the second 4 stays. (a) would remove every 4.

questions.stem: Walking a dynamic array and walking a linked list are both O(n), yet the array walk is usually several times faster. Why?
options: The array walk is really O(log n)
Each step of the list walk must update _size
The array's references are contiguous and the processor reads memory in blocks; nodes are scattered, so each next may jump elsewhere
Python copies every node as the walk reaches it
questions.explanation: It is a constant factor that Big-O hides. An array's references are contiguous, and memory is fetched in blocks (the cache). A list's nodes were created one at a time, wherever there was room. Both walks are Θ(n) (a), and walking does not touch _size (b).

questions.stem: In a circular list the last node points back to the first. What does the usual loop while node is not None: do on it?
options: It loops for ever, because no next is ever None
It visits every node once and stops
It stops when it returns to the head
questions.explanation: Every node has a successor, so node is never None and the loop never ends. A circular walk must stop when it comes back to its starting node. Nothing in the loop shown checks for that (d).

questions.stem:
What is printed?

a, b, c = Node(1), Node(2), Node(3)
a.next = b
b.next = c
b.next, c.next = None, b
print(a.next.value, c.next.value, b.next)
questions.explanation: a.next is still b, whose value is 2. The tuple assignment sets b.next = None and c.next = b, so c.next.value is 2 too, and b.next prints None. (a) reads c.next as if it still pointed forward.

questions.stem: LinkedList().pop_front():
questions.explanation: The contract raises IndexError("pop from empty list"), like list.pop(). Without the check, self.head.value would raise AttributeError (c) on None, which is W5-B3.

questions.stem: You hold a reference node to a node in the middle of a long singly linked list. Inserting a new node immediately before it costs:
options: O(n): the node before it must be found by walking from the head
questions.explanation: Inserting before a node means changing its predecessor's next, and a singly linked node has no reference back. Inserting after it is O(1) (a). A doubly linked list makes both O(1).

questions.stem:
What is printed?

ll = LinkedList()
for v in [3, 1, 2]:
    ll.push_front(v)
ll.append(ll.pop_front())
print(list(ll))
questions.explanation: Three push_front calls build [2, 1, 3] (b), since the last one pushed is first. pop_front takes the 2, and append puts it at the end: [1, 3, 2]. The front value has moved to the back, a rotation.

questions.stem: insert_at(2, x) on a singly linked list of 5 nodes. How many references held by nodes that were already in the list change?
questions.explanation: Only the node at index 1 changes its next, to the new node. The new node's own next is set as it is made. Every node after the gap is untouched (c), which is why the splice is O(1) once the walk has found prev.

questions.stem: A singly linked list with head and _tail is reversed in place. What must happen to _tail?
options: Nothing: the last node does not change
It must refer to the old first node, which can be saved before the loop
It must be found by a walk after the loop, an extra O(n)
questions.explanation: After reversing, the old first node is the last node. Saving old_head = self.head before the loop and setting self._tail = old_head after it costs O(1), so no walk is needed (c). The last node certainly changes (a), unless the list has at most one node.

essays.stem: Compare a dynamic array and a singly linked list on four operations, with their costs. For each structure, give one situation where you would choose it, and say why.
essays.answer:
OperationDynamic arraySingly linked list
read element iO(1)O(n)
insert / remove at the frontO(n)O(1)
append at the endamortised O(1)O(n), or O(1) with a tail
insert next to a node you holdO(n)O(1)
  • Choose the array when you index by position, iterate a lot, or care about memory — e.g. storing measurements you read by index. It is compact and cache-friendly.
  • Choose the list when you insert and remove at the front, or splice at positions you already hold — e.g. a stack of undo actions, the chains of a hash table. No copying, ever.

essays.stem: Explain push_front step by step with a diagram. Show what goes wrong if the two assignments are done in the other order.
essays.answer:
• Step 1: new.next = self.head — the new node points at the current first node.
  • Step 2: self.head = new — the list now starts at the new node. Then _size += 1. Two assignments: O(1).
  • Diagram: new node → old first node → … → None, with head moving from the old first node to the new one.
  • Reversed order: self.head = new first, then new.next = self.head sets new.next = new — a node pointing at itself. Nothing refers to the old first node any more, so the rest of the list is lost, and iterating loops for ever over the one node.

essays.stem: LinkedList supports ll[i], just like an array. Explain why the cost is different, and why for i in range(len(ll)): ll[i] is a bad loop. What should be written instead?
essays.answer:
• Array indexing is address arithmetic, O(1). List indexing must follow next from head i times, O(i) — the same interface hides a different cost.
  • In the loop, each ll[i] starts again from the head: 0 + 1 + … + (n-1) = O(n2) for what should be one pass.
  • Write for value in ll: — __iter__ keeps its place and walks once: O(n).

essays.stem: A tail reference makes append O(1). What does it cost? Name the methods that must change, and explain why removing the last node is still O(n).
essays.answer:
• Benefit: append links after _tail and moves _tail: O(1) instead of a walk.
  • Cost: one more reference to keep correct in every method that can change the last node: push_front and append on an empty list (the new node is also the tail), insert_at at the end, pop_front of the only node, remove of the last node, and reverse (head and tail swap).
  • Removing the last node is still O(n): _tail must move to the node before it, and in a singly linked list only a walk from the head finds that node.

essays.stem: Explain what a doubly linked list and a sentinel node each fix, and what each costs.
essays.answer:
• Doubly linked: each node also references its predecessor. Removing a node you hold, and removing from the end, become O(1); the list can be walked backwards. Cost: one more reference per node, and every insertion and removal updates twice as many links.
  • Sentinel: a permanent node before the first real one, so every real node has a predecessor and there is no special case for the head (or for an empty list). Cost: one extra node, and every method must remember that the first real node is sentinel.next.

essays.stem: A music player keeps a playlist. The user presses next and previous, and can delete the song that is playing. Which structure would you choose: a dynamic array, a singly linked list or a doubly linked list? Give the cost of each of the three actions in your choice, and say why each of the other two is worse.
essays.answer:
• Choice: a doubly linked list, holding a reference to the current node.
  • Costs: next is current = current.next, O(1). Previous is current = current.prev, O(1). Delete the current song is current.prev.next = current.next and current.next.prev = current.prev, O(1), with the head and tail handled as special cases (or a sentinel).
  • Singly linked: next is O(1), but previous and delete need the node before the current one, so they mean a walk from the head, O(n).
  • Dynamic array, holding an index: next and previous are O(1), but deleting shifts every later song left, O(n).

essays.stem: Explain insert_at(index, value) step by step: the check on index, the case index == 0, the walk, and the splice. Why does the walk stop after index - 1 steps? Give the best-case and worst-case cost, and show what goes wrong if the loop is written for _ in range(index):, both for an index in the middle and for index == len(ll).
essays.answer:
• Steps: raise IndexError unless 0 <= index <= len (index == len means "at the end"). If index == 0, call push_front, because there is no node before the gap. Otherwise walk prev from the head index - 1 steps, then prev.next = Node(value, prev.next) and _size += 1.
  • Why index - 1: only the node before the gap holds the reference that must change. It is at index index - 1, which is index - 1 steps from the head.
  • Cost: best case O(1), at index 0 or 1. Worst case O(n), at the end. The splice itself is always O(1).
  • range(index): the walk goes one node too far. insert_at(1, 9) on [1, 2, 3] gives [1, 2, 9, 3], with no error. At index == len, prev walks off the end to None, and prev.next raises AttributeError.

essays.stem: A linked list and a dynamic array are both O(n) to walk, yet measurement shows the array is faster and smaller. Explain both differences, with numbers for CPython. When is the linked list still the right choice?
essays.answer:
• Memory: an array slot is one 8-byte reference. A Node with __slots__ is about 48 bytes on 64-bit CPython, six times as much per element, plus the value object in both cases.
  • Speed: the array's references are contiguous and the processor reads memory in blocks (the cache). Nodes are scattered, so every next may jump to a new place. That is the same Big-O with a bigger constant.
  • Still the right choice: frequent insertion or removal at the front (a stack); splicing at positions you already hold (an LRU cache, an editor's buffer); never paying for a big copy at an unlucky moment; and short chains inside a hash table.

essays.stem: Explain how reverse() reverses a list in place with three references. State what prev and current mean at the start of each pass of the loop, why following must be saved first, and why the extra space is O(1). Compare with building a reversed copy with push_front.
essays.answer:
• The invariant: at the start of each pass, prev is the head of the part already reversed (None at first) and current is the head of the part still to reverse. The loop ends when current is None, and then self.head = prev.
  • Each pass: following = current.next, then current.next = prev, then prev, current = current, following. That turns one link round and moves one step forward.
  • Why save following first: once current.next points backwards, it is the only reference to the rest of the list. Without the saved copy, the rest is lost, and the loop steps back onto prev (W5-B4).
  • Space: three references, whatever n is, so O(1) extra space and O(n) time. A reversed copy built by push_front also takes O(n) time, but it makes n new nodes, which is O(n) extra space, and it leaves the original list unchanged.
